ResponsesInList.Text: Great! Thanks Georg.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Unicode
ResponsesInList.Text: Excellent! Thanks for getting back on this Georg! Yes, English is/was hardcoded for efficiency (in print_header function in lib/weblib.php). Which software are you using for the recoding?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Unicode
ResponsesInList.Text: recode 3.6, http://recode.progiciels-bpi.ca/ If possible, I would prefer that all encoding information is taken from the language packs. Forcing UTF-8 (or some other encoding) via the server is no relly good idea as users may upload html files in various encodings. Taking the encoding from the page header is the most flexible solution. As long as all moodle forms use the db encoding, things should not break (I still would prefer to have a solution where client and db can use different encodings, but I see the problems ...) There will probably also be a problem if external datasources (like ldap) use an encoding different from the moodle db. Any hints for that ? Next I will try if ldap works. Georg

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Unicode
ResponsesInList.Text: I create a Vietnamese language module (vi). Initially I leave the charset field (in moodle.php) as "iso-8859-1". The pages look OK, but when editing something in a text box (like user profile), the text appear in ASCII+ XML CharRef (i.e. Quản). It looks very disconcerting for end-users. So I set charset field to "UTF-8". Bingo! Vietnamese text shows up and appear correctly in all modes. But there is a slight problem if user choose another language for GUI. Since the course content is in Vietnamese (UTF-8), if user choose Vietnamese UI (also UTF-8) everything is fine. If user choose, let say Francais UI (iso-8859-15), the French user interface looks fine, but the course content in Vietnamese is messed up. Why would a user choose a non-Vietnamese user interface for a Vietnamese language lesson , you might ask? It's because there are nearly 3 millions oversea Vietnamese living all over the world. The Vietnamese users in France would be more comfortable with a French-language user interface than a Viet interface. The same is true for Vietnamese users in other European countries, in US, in Japan, and in Vietnam. The solution is making all language pack the same charset, in this case UTF-8, which I believe has been done. BTW , I use web hosting, linux, MySQL for Moodle. N.Tran

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Odp: Re: Unicode
ResponsesInList.Text: I'm using Czech language pack converted to UTF-8, MySQL 3.23.58 (default charset ISO-8859-2), PHP 4.3.8, database data were converted to Unicode. Forum searching works fine, is case sensitive though; the only - minor - trouble is highlighting, as Zbigniew's. I had serious trouble with alphabetical sorting of course students, moodle users, glossary entries, etc., as I cannot rely on the database query to handle the sorting with ORDER BY ; I have come to a conclusion that I would pull all required data into PHP, sort it according to LC_COLLATE, chunk it as database query would do, and then display. As an example, there is a modification of mod/glossary/sql.php (the very bottom of the file): //  $allentries = get_records_sql("$sqlselect $sqlfrom $sqlwhere $sqlorderby $sqllimit");  // Original MOODLE line $allentries = get_records_sql("$sqlselect $sqlfrom $sqlwhere $sqlorderby LIMIT 0,99999"); if ($allentries) { foreach ($allentries as $entry) { $eentries[$entry->id] = mb_convert_case($entry->concept,MB_CASE_LOWER,"UTF-8");  //We want to sort case insensitive } setlocale(LC_COLLATE, 'cs_CZ.UTF-8');  // Should be CFG->locale from the db uasort($eentries,'strcoll');  // Sorting according to LC_COLLATE foreach ($eentries as $key => $value) { $nentries[] = $allentries[$key]; } $allentries = $nentries; if ($offset != -1 and $entriesbypage > 0) {  // If $offset == 1, all entries should be shown $perpageentries = array_chunk($allentries, $entriesbypage, TRUE);  // All entries chunked into arrays with $entriesbypage users $allentries = $perpageentries[$offset/$entriesbypage];  // Entries for the given page } } It's not extremely nice but it works, the structure of the algorithm is based on Martin's code in user/index.php where I use a similar solution. Posting it here in the hope experienced PHP programmers could tell if something like this could be (after some abstraction) used at other places. Teachers at my school need multilanguage pages, tests, glossary entries, etc., so I decided to go Unicode; at the same time character sets and user defined collation support will come with MySQL 4.1.1 at te earliest (still Beta release) and my admin won't upgrade to it until it becomes astable release - so I'm looking for a possibility to offer the faculty a Unicode Moodle site before the autumn term starts. Dan

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: encoding problem
ResponsesInList.Text: The problem here is that the old pack was not actually in UTF-8 format ... it was using Numeric Character Representations where each character was created using a string in ASCII like ؘ This was causing the many problems with searching, glossaries and so on, since each character is actually 5 or 6. A proper Unicode encoding will be better, but will still have some problems, since PHP (and Moodle) don't properly handle UTF-8 yet. The most common encoding on the web for Farsi and Arabic is actually Windows-1256 ... it should work very well with Moodle ( it works automatically for me ). On your site the Apache configuration may be forcing the page encoding to be reported as Unicode or something else ... which is why your browser isn't using the encoding that is stated in the HTML code.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: U.S. English - marks vs points
ResponsesInList.Text: I think it is a good idea to discuss changes to the language files in the community before implementing them, especially with languages as widely used as U.S. English. People might be confused when their Moodle after an upgrade suddenly uses different words for the same concepts.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: U.S. English - marks vs points
ResponsesInList.Text: I think that the difference in usage of 'marks' vs 'points' is of about the same level of significance at the 'enrolment'/'enrollment' issue. To Americans, the entire effort receives a 'mark' or 'grade' but the individual items adding up to the total grade are 'points' not 'marks'. Most Americans are probably unaware of the British/Australian usage of the term. Since the total evaluation in both Am. E and Br. E can be called 'Marks' it doesn't seem strange when it is the label of a column in a summary. It's only in cases when we are talking about the total number of marks/points that a specific item should receive that the distinction is important. I vote for replacing the definition in lang/en_us/quiz.php: $string['marks'] = 'Points'; This will still work in Am. E as a column heading.

You should edit a line in your index.php file to the code I have submitted below. This may be a short-cut but it works a treat for us Regards David Keenan Instead of: if (empty($CFG->langmenu)) { $langmenu = ""; } else { $currlang = current_language(); $langs = get_list_of_languages(); $langmenu = popup_form ("$CFG-> wwwroot /?lang=", $langs, "chooselang", $currlang, "", "", "", true); } It should be: if (empty($CFG->langmenu)) { $langmenu = ""; } else { $currlang = current_language(); $langs = get_list_of_languages(); $langmenu = popup_form (" $CFG->wwwroot/index.php?lang= ", $langs, "chooselang", $currlang, "", "", "", true); }

ResponsesInList.Text: I know that the only differences showed are in the English version. That is the important point: to get the changes on ORIGINAL documents tracked in order to UPDATE the translations. The way to keep the translations updated is to translate a given version of the original file and keep informed of the changes on this original file since the time you translated it (that is, comparing the version of the translated file or even the modification date of it with the version or date of the original file). This way, you will always know which files you have to update. Regarding to know exactly what text to update or translate, you only have to see the diff between your last translated file and the last publised original file.

ResponsesInList.Title: First name?
ResponsesInList.Text: I'm having a bit of a problem with the current nomenclature on the "Profile" page for names. As most of you are aware, there are certain countries where the "First name" when talking about the actual order of names, is the surname, while the "Last name" is the given name. Cultures that use this order include Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Hungarian. If all of the students being taught are from the same culture, perhaps this isn't much of a problem, but for me, I've got students from all over the world. Those from a "surname first" culture thus need to figure out whether they should REALLY put down their first name, or whether what is meant is for them to put down their given name. Could we go for some more culturally neutral terminology here - "Surnam"e (or "family name") and "Given name"? I doubt that it would be worthwhile placing fields in the course profile or site profile saying "Your word for 'surname'" etc., would it?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: First name?
ResponsesInList.Text: Actually, the reason it says first name and last name is because I was trying to be culturally neutral (not assuming one name was a family name etc). However, now we have the fullname() function which will rearrange the names depending on site settings and language settings, it might make more sense, I guess, to call them Surname and Given name, but I'd really like to hear from others about this ... Then there's the Spanish and Arabic names, which seem to regularly use at least three public names ...

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: First name?
ResponsesInList.Text: Yes, I thought you might have been trying, but your translators weren't! I just looked at the Chinese (Taiwan & Mainland) and Japanese versions and found this: The Chinese have used the word for "Surname", "xing", where Moodle stores the "firstname" field and the word for "Given name", "ming", where Moodle stores the "lastname" field. The Japanese, however, has it the other was round.

ResponsesInList.Title: first names and last names, given names and surnames
ResponsesInList.Text:
To prevent these mixups happening in future I'm going to alter the tranlations in English to read: 
```text
  $string['lastname'] = 'Surname';


  $string['firstname'] = 'Given name(s)';
```
 and
recommend to all translators that they translate these literally. There
will then be a new string that specifies the best order to use: 
```text
  $string['fullnamedisplay'] = '$a->firstname $a->lastname';
```
 ...and all displayed names will be printed using the new fullname function for full control. If anyone has any objections, speak now, because I'm fixing this today! (I can't think of a clean way to fix existing name mixups other than
just asking all the users to visit their profile and fix their own
entry.)

ResponsesInList.Title: Improved storage of strings in language packs
ResponsesInList.Text: The language editor now saves strings files using 'single quote' strings rather than "double quote" strings. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: RTL vs LTR language setting - Just curious!
ResponsesInList.Text: Are there situations where Arabic is used LTR?  I don't know Arabic, but I do know that numbers even embedded in an LTR text are entered and read LTR but the font end processor surely takes care of this automatically. All of the rest of the RTL languages these days are ones based on either the Hebrew or Arabic scripts, Yiddish for the former and Armenian, Kurdish, Farsi, Pashto, Sindhi, and Urdu for the later. There may be some more minor ones in the former Soviet Republics that border the Arabic script-using countries to the south.  Chinese is no longer written RTL, nor is Japanese. Of the above, Farsi (Iran) and Urdu (Pakistan) are good candidates for future language modules since they are national languages with large numbers of computer users.

ResponsesInList.Title: possible solution to problem of displaying multibyte character
ResponsesInList.Text: PHPNuke is a multilanguage websit-builder package writed in php too, and its multibyte character languages work fine. It's language package files use the function define("...","...") rather than $string('...')="..." in Moodle.  In functional php files, PHPNuke calls the defined strings directly, eg echo "something"._DEFINEDSTRING."another strings"......... Can Moodle try this method?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: possible solution to problem of displaying multibyte character
ResponsesInList.Text: Well, not only would it be a big change, but Moodle's method is much more flexible than PHPNuke. It allows variable substitution on-the-fly and the ability to "fall back" to English if the string hasn't been defined yet. So no, it won't change. Which multibyte problems do you mean, anyhow? Chinese and Japanese display perfectly for me.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Concepts (words) that I don't uderstood so well
ResponsesInList.Text: (It's not a good idea to post as the Guest Teacher, others using that account will be able to edit or delete your posts). OK. The separate/connected knowing stuff is something that even English speakers would not be sure about. Which is why I wrote this help file: http://moodle.com/lang/en/help/forum/ratings.html which is referenced as a help button on forum creation and on the ratings submit button. Have a read. Does it make sense to you? Approximately, Marks == Grades == Points == Score ... except it is convention in English to say a question in a test is worth xx marks, rather than xx grades. I don't know why. In fact, here in Australia we don't even use grades much at all. In a way, yes, it's like a game, in that "marks" are made on a board and added up to produce a final "score".

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Concepts (words) that I don't uderstood so well
ResponsesInList.Text: I believe there's a bug on the issue, but I'd also like to offer that in North American "English" (same in Canada right?) "marks" is almost never used. In US-English, speakers will usually use "points" instead of marks, but talk about percentages of "grades." Both are frequently used. "I only got 50 points on that quiz, rats!" "This exam is worth 40% of your final grade." "Professor, can you give me 4 points on this question, because you worded the question so poorly?" "The grades on the exam were pretty bad on the copyright questions, so I think you guys need to reread chapter 5." I can file a bug, but I think the issue is languages should be en_US and en_AU to clarify any differences in vernacular.. Also, "cheers" to Martin... except in US-English we don't say that unless you wanna sound high-brow... so "thanks"...

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Concepts (words) that I don't uderstood so well
ResponsesInList.Text: I suspect there will even be differences of this magnitude between institutions even in one country. I don't pretend to represent Australia or the English speaking world, but I have to start somewhere! Luckily, if it bothers anyone they are free to write their own translation for Moodle (even an English one). I should point out that Moodle's expensive competitors offer no such facility. As for cheers, it's hardly meant to be high-brow when I use it! (Imagine me nodding in your direction waving a beer). Cheers! Martin

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Scores, grades etc
ResponsesInList.Text: In a "calculated" column, you can specify a mathematical formula to derive values from another column (or columns). eg (Q1 + Q2) * 0.5 In a "manual" column you'll be able to enter all grades in manually, or copy values from another column and then alter them manually. That's exactly my idea: two final columns (in califications table) with the same calculated values: the first not editable (calculated), the second (manual) with the same values of "calculated column" editable by the teacher (just in case he want to modify this value), and a save button in the end of the table that updates the final califications of students.
